Appendix B Evaluation of the atomic response functions

B.1 Useful identities

This chapter contains a number of mathematical identities necessary for the evaluation of the atomic response functions.

Spherical harmonic addition theorem

The spherical harmonics, Yℓm​(θ,ϕ)Y_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi) are given by

Yℓm​(θ,ϕ)=Nℓm​ei​m​ϕ​Pℓm​(cos⁡θ),\displaystyle Y_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi)=N_{\ell}^{m}e^{im\phi}P_{\ell}^{m}(\cos\theta)\,, (75)

where Pℓm​(cos⁡θ)P_{\ell}^{m}(\cos\theta) are the associated Legendre polynomials, and NℓmN_{\ell}^{m} is a normalization constant ensuring that ∫d​Ω​(Yℓ′m′)∗​Yℓm=δℓ​ℓ′​δm​m′\int\mathrm{d}\Omega\;(Y_{\ell^{\prime}}^{m^{\prime}})^{*}Y_{\ell}^{m}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\delta_{mm^{\prime}}. The normalization constant is given by

Nℓm\displaystyle N_{\ell}^{m} ≡2​ℓ+14​π​(ℓ−m)!(ℓ+m)!.\displaystyle\equiv\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}\frac{(\ell-m)!}{(\ell+m)!}}\,. (76)

The spherical harmonic addition theorem states that for two given unit vectors defined by the spherical angle coordinates (θ1,ϕ1)(\theta_{1},\phi_{1}) and (θ2,ϕ2)(\theta_{2},\phi_{2}), the sum over all values of mm yields [61]

∑m=−ℓℓYℓm(θ1,ϕ1)Yℓm∗(θ2,ϕ2)=2​ℓ+14​πPℓ(cosω).\displaystyle\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}Y_{\ell}^{m}(\theta_{1},\phi_{1})Y_{\ell}^{m*}(\theta_{2},\phi_{2})=\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}P_{\ell}(\cos\omega)\,. (77a)
Here, Pℓ​(x)P_{\ell}(x) is a Legendre polynomial, and ω\omega is the angle between the two vectors given by
cosω=cosθ1cosθ2+sinθ1sinθ2cos(ϕ1−ϕ2).\displaystyle\cos\omega=\cos\theta_{1}\cos\theta_{2}+\sin\theta_{1}\sin\theta_{2}\cos(\phi_{1}-\phi_{2})\,. (77b)

Plane-wave expansion

A plane-wave ei​𝐤⋅𝐱e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}} can be expressed as a linear combination of spherical waves [62],

ei​𝐤⋅𝐱=∑ℓ=0∞iℓ​(2​ℓ+1)​jℓ​(k​r)​Pℓ​(cos⁡ω),\displaystyle e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}i^{\ell}(2\ell+1)j_{\ell}(kr)P_{\ell}(\cos\omega)\,, (78a)
where ω\omega is the angle between 𝐤\mathbf{k} and 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Using the spherical harmonic addition theorem in Eq. (77), we can re-write this equation as
=4π∑ℓ=0∞iℓjℓ(kr)∑m=−ℓ+ℓYℓm∗(θk,ϕk)Yℓm(θx,ϕx).\displaystyle=4\pi\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}i^{\ell}j_{\ell}(kr)\sum_{m=-\ell}^{+\ell}Y_{\ell}^{m*}(\theta_{k},\phi_{k})\,Y_{\ell}^{m}(\theta_{x},\phi_{x})\,. (78b)

Identities with the Wigner 3j-symbol

The angular integral of the product of three spherical harmonics can be expressed in terms of the Wigner 3j-symbol [61],

∫d​Ω​Yℓ1m1​(θ,ϕ)​Yℓ2m2​(θ,ϕ)​Yℓ3m3​(θ,ϕ)=\displaystyle\int\mathrm{d}\Omega\;Y_{\ell_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\theta,\phi)Y_{\ell_{2}}^{m_{2}}(\theta,\phi)Y_{\ell_{3}}^{m_{3}}(\theta,\phi)=
=(2​ℓ1+1)​(2​ℓ2+1)​(2​ℓ3+1)4​π\displaystyle\qquad=\sqrt{\frac{(2\ell_{1}+1)(2\ell_{2}+1)(2\ell_{3}+1)}{4\pi}}
×(ℓ1ℓ2ℓ3000)​(ℓ1ℓ2ℓ3m1m2m3).\displaystyle\qquad\times\begin{pmatrix}\ell_{1}&\ell_{2}&\ell_{3}\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\ell_{1}&\ell_{2}&\ell_{3}\\ m_{1}&m_{2}&m_{3}\end{pmatrix}\,. (79)

The 3j-symbols satisfy the following orthogonality relation [62],

(2​j+1)​∑m1,m2(j1j2jm1m2m)​(j1j2j′m1m2m′)=\displaystyle(2j+1)\sum_{m_{1},m_{2}}\begin{pmatrix}j_{1}&j_{2}&j\\ m_{1}&m_{2}&m\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}j_{1}&j_{2}&j^{\prime}\\ m_{1}&m_{2}&m^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}=
=δj​j′​δm​m′​Δ​(j1,j2,j),\displaystyle\qquad=\delta_{jj^{\prime}}\delta_{mm^{\prime}}\Delta(j_{1},j_{2},j)\,, (80)

where Δ⁡(j1,j2,j)\Delta(j_{1},j_{2},j) is equal to 1 if (j1,j2,j)(j_{1},j_{2},j) satisfy the triangular condition, i.e., |j1−j2|≤j3≤j1+j2|j_{1}-j_{2}|\leq j_{3}\leq j_{1}+j_{2}, and zero otherwise.

B.2 Gradient of a wave function

In order to compute the vectorial atomic form factor in Eq. (92), we need to evaluate the gradient of a wave function ψn​l​m​(𝐱)\psi_{nlm}(\mathbf{x}) as defined in spherical coordinates (r,θ,ϕ)(r,\theta,\phi) by Eq. (37) which is given by

∇ψn​l​m​(𝐱)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\nabla}\psi_{nlm}(\mathbf{x}) =d​Rn​ℓd​r​Yℓm​(θ,ϕ)​𝐫^+\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{d}R_{n\ell}}{\mathrm{d}r}Y_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi)\;\hat{\mathbf{r}}\;+
+Rn​ℓ​(r)r​(d​Yℓmd​θ​𝜽^+1sin⁡θ​d​Yℓmd​ϕ​ϕ^),\displaystyle+\frac{R_{n\ell}(r)}{r}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}Y_{\ell}^{m}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\frac{\mathrm{d}Y_{\ell}^{m}}{\mathrm{d}\phi}\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\right)\,, (81)

with the unit vectors

𝐫^=(sin⁡θ​cos⁡ϕsin⁡θ​sin⁡ϕcos⁡θ)\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{r}}=\begin{pmatrix}\sin\theta\cos\phi\\ \sin\theta\sin\phi\\ \cos\theta\end{pmatrix} ,𝜽^=(cos⁡θ​cos⁡ϕcos⁡θ​sin⁡ϕ−sin⁡θ),\displaystyle,\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta\cos\phi\\ \cos\theta\sin\phi\\ -\sin\theta\end{pmatrix},\,
ϕ^=\displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}= (−sin⁡ϕcos⁡ϕ0).\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}-\sin\phi\\ \cos\phi\\ 0\end{pmatrix}\,. (82)

This gradient can be expressed in terms of vector spherical harmonics (VSH),

∇ψn​l​m​(𝐱)=d​Rn​ℓd​r​𝐘ℓm​(θ,ϕ)+Rn​ℓ​(r)r​𝚿ℓm​(θ,ϕ),\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\nabla}\psi_{nlm}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\mathrm{d}R_{n\ell}}{\mathrm{d}r}\mathbf{Y}_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi)+\frac{R_{n\ell}(r)}{r}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi)\,, (83)

where the VSH are defined following the conventions of Barrera et al. [63],

𝐘ℓm​(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle\mathbf{Y}_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi) ≡𝐫^​Yℓm​(θ,ϕ),\displaystyle\equiv\hat{\mathbf{r}}\,Y_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi)\,, (84a)
𝚿ℓm​(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi) ≡r∇Yℓm(θ,ϕ).\displaystyle\equiv r\,\boldsymbol{\nabla}Y_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi)\,. (84b)

The Cartesian components of the VSHs can themselves be expanded in spherical harmonics with coefficients closely related to Clebsch-Gordan coefficients [62],

(𝐘ℓm​(θ,ϕ))i=∑ℓ^=ℓ−1ℓ+1∑m^=m−1m+1cℓ^​m^(i)​Yℓ^m^​(θ,ϕ),\displaystyle\left(\mathbf{Y}_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi)\right)_{i}=\sum_{\hat{\ell}=\ell-1}^{\ell+1}\sum_{\hat{m}=m-1}^{m+1}c_{\hat{\ell}\hat{m}}^{(i)}Y_{\hat{\ell}}^{\hat{m}}(\theta,\phi)\,, (85)

with the non-vanishing coefficients

cℓ−1​m−1(1)\displaystyle c_{\ell-1\,m-1}^{(1)} =−i​cℓ−1​m−1(2)=−A−1−2​(2​ℓ−1)​(2​ℓ+1),\displaystyle=-ic_{\ell-1\,m-1}^{(2)}=-\frac{A_{-1}^{-}}{2\sqrt{(2\ell-1)(2\ell+1)}}\,,
cℓ+1​m−1(1)\displaystyle c_{\ell+1\,m-1}^{(1)} =−i​cℓ+1​m−1(2)=A−1+2​(2​ℓ+3)​(2​ℓ+1),\displaystyle=-ic_{\ell+1\,m-1}^{(2)}=\frac{A_{-1}^{+}}{2\sqrt{(2\ell+3)(2\ell+1)}}\,,
cℓ−1​m+1(1)\displaystyle c_{\ell-1\,m+1}^{(1)} =i​cℓ−1​m+1(2)=A1−2​(2​ℓ−1)​(2​ℓ+1),\displaystyle=ic_{\ell-1\,m+1}^{(2)}=\frac{A_{1}^{-}}{2\sqrt{(2\ell-1)(2\ell+1)}}\,,
cℓ+1​m+1(1)\displaystyle c_{\ell+1\,m+1}^{(1)} =i​cℓ+1​m+1(2)=−A1+2​(2​ℓ+3)​(2​ℓ+1),\displaystyle=ic_{\ell+1\,m+1}^{(2)}=-\frac{A_{1}^{+}}{2\sqrt{(2\ell+3)(2\ell+1)}}\,,
cℓ−1​m(3)\displaystyle c_{\ell-1\,m}^{(3)} =A0−2​(2​ℓ−1)​(2​ℓ+1),\displaystyle=\frac{A_{0}^{-}}{\sqrt{2(2\ell-1)(2\ell+1)}}\,,
cℓ+1​m(3)\displaystyle c_{\ell+1\,m}^{(3)} =−A0+2​(2​ℓ+3)​(2​ℓ+1).\displaystyle=-\frac{A_{0}^{+}}{\sqrt{2(2\ell+3)(2\ell+1)}}\,.

Here, we used the notation of [62],

A1+\displaystyle A_{1}^{+} =(ℓ+m+1)​(ℓ+m+2),\displaystyle=\sqrt{(\ell+m+1)(\ell+m+2)}\,, (86a)
A0+\displaystyle A_{0}^{+} =−2​(ℓ+m+1)​(ℓ−m+1),\displaystyle=-\sqrt{2(\ell+m+1)(\ell-m+1)}\,, (86b)
A−1+\displaystyle A_{-1}^{+} =(ℓ−m+1)​(ℓ−m+2),\displaystyle=\sqrt{(\ell-m+1)(\ell-m+2)}\,, (86c)
A1−\displaystyle A_{1}^{-} =(ℓ−m−1)​(ℓ−m),\displaystyle=\sqrt{(\ell-m-1)(\ell-m)}\,, (86d)
A0−\displaystyle A_{0}^{-} =2​(ℓ+m)​(ℓ−m),\displaystyle=\sqrt{2(\ell+m)(\ell-m)}\,, (86e)
A−1−\displaystyle A_{-1}^{-} =(ℓ+m−1)​(ℓ+m).\displaystyle=\sqrt{(\ell+m-1)(\ell+m)}\,. (86f)

Similarly, the second VSH can be expanded as

(𝚿ℓm​(θ,ϕ))i=∑ℓ^=ℓ−1ℓ+1∑m^=m−1m+1dℓ^​m^(i)​Yℓ^m^​(θ,ϕ),\displaystyle\left(\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi)\right)_{i}=\sum_{\hat{\ell}=\ell-1}^{\ell+1}\sum_{\hat{m}=m-1}^{m+1}d_{\hat{\ell}\hat{m}}^{(i)}Y_{\hat{\ell}}^{\hat{m}}(\theta,\phi)\,, (87)

with coefficients,

dℓ−1​m−1(1)\displaystyle d_{\ell-1\,m-1}^{(1)} =−i​dℓ−1​m−1(2)=−(ℓ+1)​A−1−2​(2​ℓ+1)​(2​ℓ−1),\displaystyle=-id_{\ell-1\,m-1}^{(2)}=-\frac{(\ell+1)A_{-1}^{-}}{2\sqrt{(2\ell+1)(2\ell-1)}}\,,
dℓ+1​m−1(1)\displaystyle d_{\ell+1\,m-1}^{(1)} =−i​dℓ+1​m−1(2)=−ℓ​A−1+2​(2​ℓ+1)​(2​ℓ+3),\displaystyle=-id_{\ell+1\,m-1}^{(2)}=-\frac{\ell\,A_{-1}^{+}}{2\sqrt{(2\ell+1)(2\ell+3)}}\,,
dℓ−1​m+1(1)\displaystyle d_{\ell-1\,m+1}^{(1)} =i​dℓ−1​m+1(2)=(ℓ+1)​A1−2​(2​ℓ+1)​(2​ℓ−1),\displaystyle=id_{\ell-1\,m+1}^{(2)}=\frac{(\ell+1)A_{1}^{-}}{2\sqrt{(2\ell+1)(2\ell-1)}}\,,
dℓ+1​m+1(1)\displaystyle d_{\ell+1\,m+1}^{(1)} =i​dℓ+1​m+1(2)=ℓ​A1+2​(2​ℓ+1)​(2​ℓ+3),\displaystyle=id_{\ell+1\,m+1}^{(2)}=\frac{\ell\,A_{1}^{+}}{2\sqrt{(2\ell+1)(2\ell+3)}}\,,
dℓ−1​m(3)\displaystyle d_{\ell-1\,m}^{(3)} =(ℓ+1)​A0−2​(2​ℓ+1)​(2​ℓ−1),\displaystyle=\frac{(\ell+1)A_{0}^{-}}{\sqrt{2(2\ell+1)(2\ell-1)}}\,,
dℓ+1​m(3)\displaystyle d_{\ell+1\,m}^{(3)} =ℓ​A0+2​(2​ℓ+1)​(2​ℓ+3).\displaystyle=\frac{\ell\,A_{0}^{+}}{\sqrt{2(2\ell+1)(2\ell+3)}}\,.

Eqs. (85) and (87) allow us to the express the gradient of the wave function ψl​m​n\psi_{lmn} in a compact expansion in spherical harmonics,

∇ψn​l​m​(𝐱)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\nabla}\psi_{nlm}(\mathbf{x}) =∑i=13𝐞i∑ℓ^=ℓ−1ℓ+1∑m^=m−1m+1\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\mathbf{e}_{i}\sum_{\hat{\ell}=\ell-1}^{\ell+1}\sum_{\hat{m}=m-1}^{m+1}
(cℓ^​m^(i)​d​Rn​ℓd​r+dℓ^​m^(i)​Rn​ℓ​(r)r)​Yℓ^m^​(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle\left(c_{\hat{\ell}\hat{m}}^{(i)}\frac{\mathrm{d}R_{n\ell}}{\mathrm{d}r}+d_{\hat{\ell}\hat{m}}^{(i)}\frac{R_{n\ell}(r)}{r}\right)Y_{\hat{\ell}}^{\hat{m}}(\theta,\phi) (88)

where 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i}, (i=1,2,3i=1,2,3) are the three Cartesian unit vectors.

B.3 The atomic form factors

In Eqs. (24) and (26), we introduced the scalar and vectorial atomic form factors. In this section, we describe the details of evaluting these form factors.

First, we denote the initial (‘1’) and final (‘2’) state electron wave functions by their respective quantum numbers (n,ℓ,m)(n,\ell,m) and (k′,ℓ′,m′)(k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime},m^{\prime}). Consequently, the atomic form factors take the form

f1→2​(𝐪)\displaystyle f_{1\rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{q}) =∫d3​k(2​π)3​ψk′​ℓ′​m′∗​(𝐤+𝐪)​ψn​l​m​(𝐤),\displaystyle=\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\psi^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q})\psi_{nlm}(\mathbf{k})\,, (89)
𝐟1→2​(𝐪)\displaystyle\mathbf{f}_{1\rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{q}) =∫d3​k(2​π)3​ψk′​ℓ′​m′∗​(𝐤+𝐪)​𝐤me​ψn​l​m​(𝐤).\displaystyle=\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\psi^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q})\;\frac{\mathbf{k}}{m_{e}}\;\psi_{nlm}(\mathbf{k})\,. (90)

Moving to position space via a Fourier transformation, we find

f1→2​(𝐪)\displaystyle f_{1\rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{q}) =∫d3​x​ψk′​ℓ′​m′∗​(𝐱)​ei​𝐱⋅𝐪​ψn​ℓ​m​(𝐱),\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}^{3}x\;\psi^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x})e^{i\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{q}}\psi_{n\ell m}(\mathbf{x})\,, (91)
𝐟1→2​(𝐪)\displaystyle\mathbf{f}_{1\rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{q}) =∫d3​x​ψk′​ℓ′​m′∗​(𝐱)​ei​𝐱⋅𝐪​i∇me​ψn​ℓ​m​(𝐱).\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}^{3}x\;\psi^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x})e^{i\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{q}}\frac{i\boldsymbol{\nabla}}{m_{e}}\psi_{n\ell m}(\mathbf{x})\,. (92)

In Eqs. (37) and (38) we expressed the initial and final state electron wave functions in terms of spherical coordinates 𝐱⁡(r,θ,ϕ)\mathbf{x}(r,\theta,\phi), where the angular dependence is given by the spherical harmonics,

ψn​ℓ​m​(𝐱)=Rn​ℓ​(r)​Yℓm​(θ,ϕ).\displaystyle\psi_{n\ell m}(\mathbf{x})=R_{n\ell}(r)\,Y_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi)\,. (93)

We postpone the discussion of the radial components of the wave functions to Appendix B.4. and start with the evaluation of the scalar atomic form factor f1→2f_{1\rightarrow 2}. Afterwards, we discuss the vectorial atomic form factor 𝐟1→2\mathbf{f}_{1\rightarrow 2}.

Scalar atomic form factor

Focussing on the scalar atomic form factor for now, we replace the exponential ei​𝐱⋅𝐪e^{i\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{q}} with the plane-wave expansion of Eq. (78).

f1→2​(𝐪)\displaystyle f_{1\rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{q}) =∫d3xRk′​ℓ′∗(r)Yℓ′m′∗(θ,ϕ)Rn​ℓ(r)Yℓm(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}^{3}x\;R^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}(r)Y_{\ell^{\prime}}^{m^{\prime}*}(\theta,\phi)R_{n\ell}(r)Y_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi)
×4π∑L=0∞iLjL(qr)∑M=−L+LYLM∗(θq,ϕq)YLM(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle\times 4\pi\sum_{L=0}^{\infty}i^{L}j_{L}(qr)\sum_{M=-L}^{+L}Y_{L}^{M*}(\theta_{q},\phi_{q})\,Y_{L}^{M}(\theta,\phi)
=4π∑L=0∞iL∑M=−LLI1(q)YLM∗(θq,ϕq)\displaystyle=4\pi\sum_{L=0}^{\infty}i^{L}\sum_{M=-L}^{L}I_{1}(q)Y_{L}^{M*}(\theta_{q},\phi_{q})
×∫dΩYℓ′m′∗(θ,ϕ)Yℓm(θ,ϕ)YLM(θ,ϕ),\displaystyle\times\int\mathrm{d}\Omega\;Y_{\ell^{\prime}}^{m^{\prime}*}(\theta,\phi)Y_{\ell}^{m}(\theta,\phi)Y_{L}^{M}(\theta,\phi)\,, (94)

where we absorbed the radial integral into

I1​(q)≡∫d​r​r2​Rk′​ℓ′∗​(r)​Rn​ℓ​(r)​jL​(q​r).\displaystyle I_{1}(q)\equiv\int\mathrm{d}r\;r^{2}R^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}(r)R_{n\ell}(r)j_{L}(qr)\,. (95)

This integral is the spherical Bessel transform of Rk′​ℓ′∗​(r)​Rn​ℓ​(r)R^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}(r)R_{n\ell}(r), i.e. the product of the radial components of the final and initial wave functions. For its evaluation, we refer to Appendix B.5.

The integral over three spherical harmonics in the last expression can be re-written in terms of the Wigner 3j-symbols via Eq. (79),

f1→2​(𝐪)\displaystyle f_{1\rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{q}) =4​π∑L=|ℓ−ℓ′|ℓ+ℓ′iLI1(q)∑M=−L+LYLM∗(θq,ϕq)\displaystyle=\sqrt{4\pi}\sum_{L=|\ell-\ell^{\prime}|}^{\ell+\ell^{\prime}}i^{L}I_{1}(q)\sum_{M=-L}^{+L}Y_{L}^{M*}(\theta_{q},\phi_{q})
×(−1)m′​(2​ℓ+1)​(2​ℓ′+1)​(2​L+1)​(ℓℓ′L000)\displaystyle\times(-1)^{m^{\prime}}\sqrt{(2\ell+1)(2\ell^{\prime}+1)(2L+1)}\begin{pmatrix}\ell&\ell^{\prime}&L\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}
×(ℓℓ′Lm−m′M).\displaystyle\times\begin{pmatrix}\ell&\ell^{\prime}&L\\ m&-m^{\prime}&M\end{pmatrix}\,. (96)

At this point, we can already evaluate the first atomic response W1n​ℓW_{1}^{n\ell} given by Eq. (41a), which essentially given by the squared modulus of the scalar atomic form factor summed over m,m′m,m^{\prime},

∑m=−ℓℓ\displaystyle\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell} ∑m′=−ℓ′ℓ′|f1→2​(𝐪)|2=∑m​m′4​π​∑L​L′iL​(−i)L′​|I1​(q)|2\displaystyle\sum_{m^{\prime}=-\ell^{\prime}}^{\ell^{\prime}}\left|f_{1\rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{q})\right|^{2}=\sum_{mm^{\prime}}4\pi\sum_{LL^{\prime}}i^{L}(-i)^{L^{\prime}}\left|I_{1}(q)\right|^{2}
×∑M,M′YLM∗(θq,ϕq)YL′M′(θq,ϕq)\displaystyle\times\sum_{M,M^{\prime}}Y_{L}^{M*}(\theta_{q},\phi_{q})Y_{L^{\prime}}^{M^{\prime}}(\theta_{q},\phi_{q})
×(2​ℓ+1)​(2​ℓ′+1)​(2​L+1)​(2​L′+1)\displaystyle\times(2\ell+1)(2\ell^{\prime}+1)\sqrt{(2L+1)(2L^{\prime}+1)}
×(ℓℓ′L000)​(ℓℓ′L′000)\displaystyle\times\begin{pmatrix}\ell&\ell^{\prime}&L\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\ell&\ell^{\prime}&L^{\prime}\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}
×(ℓℓ′Lm−m′M)​(ℓℓ′L′m−m′M′).\displaystyle\times\begin{pmatrix}\ell&\ell^{\prime}&L\\ m&-m^{\prime}&M\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\ell&\ell^{\prime}&L^{\prime}\\ m&-m^{\prime}&M^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}\,. (97)

The orthogonality of the Wigner 3j-symbols, Eq. (80), allows us to sum over the L′L^{\prime} and M′M^{\prime} indexes,

∑m=−ℓℓ∑m′=−ℓ′ℓ′|f1→2​(𝐪)|2\displaystyle\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}\sum_{m^{\prime}=-\ell^{\prime}}^{\ell^{\prime}}\left|f_{1\rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{q})\right|^{2} =4π∑LI1(q)2∑MYLM∗(θq,ϕq)\displaystyle=4\pi\sum_{L}I_{1}(q)^{2}\sum_{M}Y_{L}^{M*}(\theta_{q},\phi_{q})
×YLM​(θq,ϕq)​(2​ℓ+1)​(2​ℓ′+1)\displaystyle\times Y_{L}^{M}(\theta_{q},\phi_{q})(2\ell+1)(2\ell^{\prime}+1)
×(ℓℓ′L000)2.\displaystyle\times\begin{pmatrix}\ell&\ell^{\prime}&L\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}^{2}\,. (98)

Lastly we apply the spherical harmonic addition theorem given in Eq. (77),

∑m=−ℓℓ∑m′=−ℓ′ℓ′|f1→2​(q)|2\displaystyle\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}\sum_{m^{\prime}=-\ell^{\prime}}^{\ell^{\prime}}\left|f_{1\rightarrow 2}(q)\right|^{2} =∑L=|ℓ−ℓ′|ℓ+ℓ′(2​ℓ+1)​(2​ℓ′+1)\displaystyle=\sum_{L=|\ell-\ell^{\prime}|}^{\ell+\ell^{\prime}}(2\ell+1)(2\ell^{\prime}+1)
×(2​L+1)​|I1​(q)|2​(ℓℓ′L000)2.\displaystyle\hskip-30.00005pt\times(2L+1)\left|I_{1}(q)\right|^{2}\begin{pmatrix}\ell&\ell^{\prime}&L\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}^{2}\,. (99)

Note that the dependence on the momentum transfer’s direction has disappeared. The explicit form of the first atomic response W1n​ℓ​(q,k′)W_{1}^{n\ell}(q,k^{\prime}) for an atomic orbital (n,ℓ)(n,\ell) given by Eq. (41a) (or equivalently the ‘ionization form factor |fionn,ℓ|2|f_{\rm ion}^{n,\ell}|^{2} defined in Eq. (35)) is obtained by adding the remainder of the final state phase space1111 11 Regarding the numerical evaluation of the sum over ℓ′\ell^{\prime}, we sum up contributions up to ℓmax′=7\ell^{\prime}_{\rm max}=7., see Eq. (27),

W1n​ℓ​(q,k′)\displaystyle W_{1}^{n\ell}(q,k^{\prime}) =V​4​k′3(2​π)3​∑ℓ′=0∞∑L=|ℓ−ℓ′|ℓ+ℓ′(2​ℓ+1)​(2​ℓ′+1)\displaystyle=V\frac{4k^{\prime 3}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=0}^{\infty}\sum_{L=|\ell-\ell^{\prime}|}^{\ell+\ell^{\prime}}(2\ell+1)(2\ell^{\prime}+1)
×(2​L+1)​|I1​(q)|2​(ℓℓ′L000)2.\displaystyle\times(2L+1)|I_{1}(q)|^{2}\begin{pmatrix}\ell&\ell^{\prime}&L\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}^{2}\,. (100)

In order to evaluate the three new atomic responses we need to follow similar steps for the vectorial atomic form factor as for the scalar one.

Vectorial atomic form factor

We start from Eq. (92) and substitute the gradient of the initial wave function using Eq. (88),

𝐟1→2​(𝐪)\displaystyle\mathbf{f}_{1\rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{q}) =ime∑i=13𝐞i∑ℓ^=ℓ−1ℓ+1∑m^=m−1m+1∫d3xRk′​ℓ′∗(r)Yℓ′m′∗(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle=\frac{i}{m_{e}}\sum_{i=1}^{3}\mathbf{e}_{i}\sum_{\hat{\ell}=\ell-1}^{\ell+1}\sum_{\hat{m}=m-1}^{m+1}\int\mathrm{d}^{3}xR^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}(r)Y^{m^{\prime}*}_{\ell^{\prime}}(\theta,\phi)
×ei​𝐱⋅𝐪​(cℓ^​m^(i)​d​Rn​ℓd​r+dℓ^​m^(i)​Rn​ℓ​(r)r)​Yℓ^m^​(θ,ϕ).\displaystyle\times e^{i\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{q}}\,\left(c_{\hat{\ell}\hat{m}}^{(i)}\frac{\mathrm{d}R_{n\ell}}{\mathrm{d}r}+d_{\hat{\ell}\hat{m}}^{(i)}\frac{R_{n\ell}(r)}{r}\right)Y_{\hat{\ell}}^{\hat{m}}(\theta,\phi)\,. (101)

As for the scalar atomic form factor, the exponential in the above equation can be expressed in terms of spherical harmonics via Eq. (78),

𝐟1→2​(𝐪)\displaystyle\mathbf{f}_{1\rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{q}) =4​π​ime∑i=13𝐞^i∑ℓ^=ℓ−1ℓ+1∑m^=m−1m+1∑L=0∞∑M=−LLYLM∗(θq,ϕq)\displaystyle=\frac{4\pi i}{m_{e}}\sum_{i=1}^{3}\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{i}\sum_{\hat{\ell}=\ell-1}^{\ell+1}\sum_{\hat{m}=m-1}^{m+1}\sum_{L=0}^{\infty}\sum_{M=-L}^{L}Y_{L}^{M*}(\theta_{q},\phi_{q})
×iL∫dΩYℓ′m′∗(θ,ϕ)YLM(θ,ϕ)Yℓ^m^(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle\times i^{L}\int\mathrm{d}\Omega\;Y^{m^{\prime}*}_{\ell^{\prime}}(\theta,\phi)Y^{M}_{L}(\theta,\phi)Y^{\hat{m}}_{\hat{\ell}}(\theta,\phi)
×[cℓ^​m^(i)​I2​(q)+dℓ^​m^(i)​I3​(q)],\displaystyle\times\left[c_{\hat{\ell}\hat{m}}^{(i)}I_{2}(q)+d_{\hat{\ell}\hat{m}}^{(i)}I_{3}(q)\right]\,, (102)

where we defined two new radial integrals,

I2​(q)\displaystyle I_{2}(q) ≡∫d​r​r2​jL​(q​r)​Rk′​ℓ′∗​(r)​d​Rn​ℓd​r,\displaystyle\equiv\int\mathrm{d}r\,r^{2}j_{L}(qr)R^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}(r)\frac{\mathrm{d}R_{n\ell}}{\mathrm{d}r}\,, (103)
I3​(q)\displaystyle I_{3}(q) ≡∫d​r​r​jL​(q​r)​Rk′​ℓ′∗​(r)​Rn​ℓ​(r),\displaystyle\equiv\int\mathrm{d}r\,rj_{L}(qr)R^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}(r)R_{n\ell}(r)\,, (104)

which will require extra attention in Appendix B.5.

We again apply Eq. (79) to explicitly perform the angular integral,

We explicitly checked that this choice of coordinate frame has no impact on the final values of the atomic response functions.

With the scalar and vectorial atomic form factors given in the forms of Eqs. (96) and (106), it is possible to evaluate the three new atomic response functions given by the Eqs. (41b) to (41d). However, before doing so, we have to specify the radial components of the initial and final state electron wave functions without which we cannot evaluate the radial integrals defined in Eqs. (95), (103), and (104).

B.4 Initial and final state wave functions

For the radial part of the initial state wave function ψn​ℓ​m​(𝐱)\psi_{n\ell m}(\mathbf{x}), we assume Roothaan-Hartree-Fock (RHF) ground state wave functions expressed as linear combinations of Slater-type orbitals,

Rn​ℓ​(r)\displaystyle R_{n\ell}(r) =a0−3/2∑jCj​ℓ​n(2​Zj​ℓ)nj​ℓ′+1/2(2​nj​ℓ′)!\displaystyle=a_{0}^{-3/2}\sum_{j}C_{j\ell n}\frac{\left(2Z_{j\ell}\right)^{n_{j\ell}^{\prime}+1/2}}{\sqrt{\left(2n_{j\ell}^{\prime}\right)!}}
×(ra0)nj​ℓ′−1​exp⁡(−Zj​ℓ​ra0).\displaystyle\times\left(\frac{r}{a_{0}}\right)^{n_{j\ell}^{\prime}-1}\exp\left(-Z_{j\ell}\frac{r}{a_{0}}\right)\,. (107)

The coefficients Cj​ℓ​nC_{j\ell n}, Zj​ℓZ_{j\ell}, and nj​ℓ′n^{\prime}_{j\ell} are tabulated for the atomic orbitals of argon and xenon in [47] together with their respective binding energies EBn​ℓE_{B}^{n\ell}. Furthermore, a0a_{0} denotes the Bohr radius.

The final electron state is described by a positive energy continuum solution of the Schrödinger equation with a hydrogenic potential −Zeff/r-Z_{\rm eff}/r [64, 12].

Rk′​ℓ′​(r)\displaystyle R_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}(r) =(2​π)3/2V​(2​k′​r)ℓ′​2π​|Γ⁡(ℓ′+1−i​Zeffk′​a0)|​eπ​Zeff2​k′​a0(2​ℓ′+1)!\displaystyle=\frac{(2\pi)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{V}}(2k^{\prime}r)^{\ell^{\prime}}\frac{\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left|\Gamma\left(\ell^{\prime}+1-\frac{iZ_{\mathrm{eff}}}{k^{\prime}a_{0}}\right)\right|e^{\frac{\pi Z_{\mathrm{eff}}}{2k^{\prime}a_{0}}}}{(2\ell^{\prime}+1)!}
×e−i​k′​r​F11​(ℓ′+1+i​Zeffk′​a0,2​ℓ′+2,2​i​k′​r).\displaystyle\hskip-20.00003pt\times e^{-ik^{\prime}r}{}_{1}F_{1}\left(\ell^{\prime}+1+\frac{iZ_{\rm eff}}{k^{\prime}a_{0}},2\ell^{\prime}+2,2ik^{\prime}r\right)\,. (108)

Here, F11​(a,b,z){}_{1}F_{1}\left(a,b,z\right) is the so-called Kummer’s function, or confluent hypergeometric function of the first kind. Note that both radial wave functions are purely real. It should also be noted that the factor of 1/V1/\sqrt{V} involving the volume always cancels due to the application of the integral operator in Eq. (27), or equivalently with the factor of VV in Eqs. (41a) to (41d).

The factor ZeffZ_{\rm eff} is determined by matching the binding energy EBn​ℓE_{B}^{n\ell} of the ionized orbital [13, 14, 20],

EBn​ℓ\displaystyle E_{B}^{n\ell} =!13.6​ eV​(Zeffn​ℓ)2n2,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle!}}{{=}}13.6\text{ eV}\frac{\left(Z_{\rm eff}^{n\ell}\right)^{2}}{n^{2}}\,,
⇒Zeffn​ℓ\displaystyle\Rightarrow Z_{\rm eff}^{n\ell} =EBn​ℓ13.6​ eV×n.\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{E_{B}^{n\ell}}{13.6\text{ eV}}}\;\times\;n\,. (109)

With the definition of the radial parts of the wave functions in place, we can continue with the evaluation of the radial integrals.

B.5 Numerical evaluation of the radial integrals

It is fair to say that the largest obstacle to the evaluation of the scalar and vectorial atomic form factors is the computation of the radial integrals1212 12 These types of integrals are known in the mathematical literature as spherical Bessel and Hankel transforms.

I1​(q)\displaystyle I_{1}(q) =∫0∞d​r​r2​jL​(q​r)​Rk′​ℓ′∗​(r)​Rn​ℓ​(r),\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}r\;r^{2}j_{L}(qr)R^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}(r)R_{n\ell}(r)\,, (110)
I2​(q)\displaystyle I_{2}(q) =∫0∞d​r​r2​jL​(q​r)​Rk′​ℓ′∗​(r)​d​Rn​ℓd​r,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}r\;r^{2}j_{L}(qr)R^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}(r)\frac{\mathrm{d}R_{n\ell}}{\mathrm{d}r}\,, (111)
I3​(q)\displaystyle I_{3}(q) =∫0∞d​r​r​jL​(q​r)​Rk′​ℓ′∗​(r)​Rn​ℓ​(r).\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}r\;rj_{L}(qr)R^{*}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}(r)R_{n\ell}(r)\,. (112)

The highly oscillatory behavior of the spherical Bessel function can hinder the success of standard numerical integration methods, especially for large values of qq.

Below, we outline two of the methods we used to solve this integral. The first one is exact, but requires the numerical integration of an oscillating function, the second one is approximate, but fully analytical.

The python code we used for the evaluation of the radial integrals, the atomic form factors, and the atomic response functions is publicly available [44].

Numerical solution

One of the most straight-forward ways to evaluate the radial integrals is the use of specific numerical integration methods of numerical libraries like e.g. NumPy [57], or computer algebra systems such as Wolfram Mathematica [60]. The numerical integration method “DoubleExponential” of the Wolfram language yielded reliable results. However, for large values of the momentum transfer, the method becomes critically slow.

It is usually beneficial for the performance of the numerical integration to split up the integration domain,

∫0∞d​r​f​(r)=∑i=0∞∫i​Δ​r(i+1)​Δ​rd​r​f​(r)\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}r\;f(r)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\int_{i\Delta r}^{(i+1)\Delta r}\mathrm{d}r\;f(r) (113)

with Δ​r=a0\Delta r=a_{0} and truncate the sum at a finite ii after the result has converged to a desired tolerance. Since the integrand in our case is highly oscillatory and this method does not ensure that we integrate from one root to the next, it is possible that an accidental cancellation of positive and negative contributions over one sub-interval of the domain can be misinterpreted as convergence. To avoid this subtle problem, we always verify the series’ convergence on two consecutive terms.

Analytic solution

The second method effectively replaces the integral with an infinite sum, which, if it converges sufficiently fast, yields accurate and prompt results. This method worked best when applied to large values of qq, i.e., exactly where the numerical integration is problematic.

The Kummer function (or confluent hypergeometric function of the first kind), which appears in Eq. (108), can be written as a power series,

F11​(a,b,z)\displaystyle{}_{1}F_{1}\left(a,b,z\right) =∑s=0∞a(s)b(s)​zss!=∑s=0∞Γ⁡(s+a)​Γ​(b)Γ⁡(a)​Γ​(s+b)​zss!,\displaystyle=\sum_{s=0}^{\infty}\frac{a^{(s)}}{b^{(s)}}\frac{z^{s}}{s!}=\sum_{s=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(s+a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(s+b)}\frac{z^{s}}{s!}\,, (114)

with x(s)≡x⁡(x+1)​…​(x+s−1)x^{(s)}\equiv x(x+1)\ldots(x+s-1) being the rising factorial. In combination with the analytic form of the initial wave function in Eq. (107), we find that the above radial integrals are infinite sums of simpler integrals of the form

IL​(q,α,β)=∫d​r​rα​exp⁡(−β​r)​jL​(q​r),\displaystyle I_{L}(q,\alpha,\beta)=\int\mathrm{d}r\;r^{\alpha}\exp(-\beta r)j_{L}(qr)\,, (115)

where the values of the parameters α\alpha and β\beta depend on whether we evaluate I1​(q)I_{1}(q), I2​(q)I_{2}(q) or I3​(q)I_{3}(q). Importantly, this integral can be solved analytically (provided that ℜ⁡(L+α)>−1\Re(L+\alpha)>-1),

IL​(q,α,β)=π​qL2L+1​βα+L+1​Γ⁡(L+α+1)Γ⁡(L+32)\displaystyle I_{L}(q,\alpha,\beta)=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}q^{L}}{2^{L+1}\beta^{\alpha+L+1}}\frac{\Gamma(L+\alpha+1)}{\Gamma\left(L+\frac{3}{2}\right)}
×F12​((L+α+1)2,(L+α+2)2,L+32,−q2β2)\displaystyle\times{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\frac{(L+\alpha+1)}{2},\frac{(L+\alpha+2)}{2},L+\frac{3}{2},-\frac{q^{2}}{\beta^{2}}\right)\, (116)

where the hypergeometric function F12​(a,b,c,z){}_{2}F_{1}\left(a,b,c,z\right) appears which is defined via

F12​(a,b,c,z)≡∑s=0∞a(s)​b(s)c(s)​zss!.\displaystyle{}_{2}F_{1}\left(a,b,c,z\right)\equiv\sum_{s=0}^{\infty}\frac{a^{(s)}b^{(s)}}{c^{(s)}}\frac{z^{s}}{s!}\,. (117)

Provided that the sum in Eq. (114) converges after a finite number of terms, we can compute the radial integrals analytically. For large qq the convergence occurs quickly. For lower values, we run into numerical precision problems, since we have to include very large numbers of terms of (114). In this case, the numerical approach described in the previous section performs better.

As an example, by using the analytical method described here, the first radial integral, I1I_{1}(q), can now be written as follows:

I1​(q)\displaystyle I_{1}(q) =∑s=0∞∑j4​π​(2​k′)ℓ′(2​ℓ′+1)!​|Γ⁡(l+1−i​Zeffk​a0)|​eπ​Zeff2​k​a0\displaystyle=\sum_{s=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j}\frac{4\pi(2k^{\prime})^{\ell^{\prime}}}{(2\ell^{\prime}+1)!}\left|\Gamma\left(l+1-\frac{iZ_{\mathrm{eff}}}{ka_{0}}\right)\right|e^{\frac{\pi Z_{\mathrm{eff}}}{2ka_{0}}}
×Cj​l​n​(2​Zj​l)(nj​l′+1/2)a0(nj​l′+1/2)​(2​nj​l′)!​Γ⁡(s+a)​Γ​(b)Γ⁡(s+b)​Γ​(a)​(2​i​k′)ss!\displaystyle\times\frac{C_{jln}(2Z_{jl})^{(n^{\prime}_{jl}+1/2)}}{a_{0}^{(n^{\prime}_{jl}+1/2)}\sqrt{(2n^{\prime}_{jl})!}}\frac{\Gamma(s+a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(s+b)\Gamma(a)}\frac{(2ik^{\prime})^{s}}{s!}
×π​qL2L+1​βα+L+1​γ⁡(L+α+1)Γ⁡(L+3/2)\displaystyle\times\frac{\sqrt{\pi}q^{L}}{2^{L+1}\beta^{\alpha+L+1}}\frac{\gamma(L+\alpha+1)}{\Gamma(L+3/2)}
×F12​(L+α+12,L+α+22,L+3/2,−q2β2),\displaystyle\times{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\frac{L+\alpha+1}{2},\frac{L+\alpha+2}{2},L+3/2,-\frac{q^{2}}{\beta^{2}}\right)\,, (118)

where we defined

α\displaystyle\alpha =1+ℓ′+nj​l′+s,β=Zj​la0+i​k′,\displaystyle=1+\ell^{\prime}+n^{\prime}_{jl}+s\,,\quad\beta=\frac{Z_{jl}}{a_{0}}+ik^{\prime}\,, (119)
a\displaystyle a =l′+1+i​Zeffk′​a0,b=2​ℓ′+1.\displaystyle=l^{\prime}+1+\frac{iZ_{\rm eff}}{k^{\prime}a_{0}}\,,\quad b=2\ell^{\prime}+1\,. (120)

The sum can be truncated when the series converges to a given tolerance, provided that it converges sufficiently quickly.

Appendix C Scattering kinematics

In this appendix, we summarize a few basic kinematic relations for DM-electron scatterings.

The initial and final energies of the inelastic scattering process are given in Eqs. (4) and (5). By the conservation of energy one can show that

𝐯⋅𝐪=Δ​E1→2+q22​mχ.\displaystyle\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{q}=\Delta E_{1\rightarrow 2}+\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{\chi}}\,. (121)

From this expression, it is clear that for a given momentum transfer qq, the minimum DM speed necessary for an electron ionization with Δ​E1→2=EB+k′2/(2​me)\Delta E_{1\rightarrow 2}=E_{B}+k^{\prime 2}/(2m_{e}) can be obtained by setting cos⁡θq​v=1\cos\theta_{qv}=1,

vmin​(k′,q)\displaystyle v_{\rm min}(k^{\prime},q) =EB+k′2/(2​me)q+q2​mχ.\displaystyle=\frac{E_{B}+k^{\prime 2}/(2m_{e})}{q}+\frac{q}{2m_{\chi}}\,. (122)

Since the local DM velocity distribution of the galactic halo is assumed to have a maximum speed vescv_{\rm esc}, DM particles are only able to ionize a bound electron with binding energy EBE_{B} if vmin<vmax=vesc+v⊕v_{\rm min}<v_{\rm max}=v_{\rm esc}+v_{\oplus}. Thereby, we find the range of momentum transfers which can contribute to the ionization,

qmin\displaystyle q_{\rm min} =mχ​vmax−mχ2​vmax2−2​mχ​EB,\displaystyle=m_{\chi}v_{\rm max}-\sqrt{m_{\chi}^{2}v_{\rm max}^{2}-2m_{\chi}E_{B}}\,, (123)
=EBvmax,for ​mχ→∞,\displaystyle=\frac{E_{B}}{v_{\rm max}}\,,\quad\text{for }m_{\chi}\rightarrow\infty\,, (124)
qmax\displaystyle q_{\rm max} =mχ​vmax+mχ2​vmax2−2​mχ​EB.\displaystyle=m_{\chi}v_{\rm max}+\sqrt{m_{\chi}^{2}v_{\rm max}^{2}-2m_{\chi}E_{B}}\,. (125)

From the requirement that vmin<vmax=vesc+v⊕v_{\rm min}<v_{\rm max}=v_{\rm esc}+v_{\oplus}, we can also derive the maximum final momentum of the electron for a given momentum transfer qq,

k′\displaystyle k^{\prime} <2​me​(vmax​q−q22​mχ+EB),\displaystyle<\sqrt{2m_{e}\left(v_{\rm max}q-\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{\chi}}+E_{B}\right)}\,, (126)

which were shown as white lines in Figs. 3 and 4.

Finally, there are a few identities involving 𝐯el⟂\mathbf{v}_{\rm el}^{\perp}, which are necessary for the evaluation of the DM response functions in the Eqs. (40). We can write 𝐯el⟂\mathbf{v}_{\rm el}^{\perp} as

𝐯el⟂\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{\rm el}^{\perp} =𝐯−𝐪2​μe−𝐤me.\displaystyle=\mathbf{v}-\frac{\mathbf{q}}{2\mu_{e}}-\frac{\mathbf{k}}{m_{e}}\,. (127)

Hence the square of the 𝐯el⟂\mathbf{v}_{\rm el}^{\perp} (with 𝐤=𝟎\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{0}) is given by

(𝐯el⟂)2|𝐤=𝟎\displaystyle(\mathbf{v}_{\rm el}^{\perp})^{2}|_{\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{0}} =v2+q24​μe2​mχ−meme+mχ−Δ​E1→2μe.\displaystyle=v^{2}+\frac{q^{2}}{4\mu_{e}^{2}}\frac{m_{\chi}-m_{e}}{m_{e}+m_{\chi}}-\frac{\Delta E_{1\rightarrow 2}}{\mu_{e}}\,. (128)

We will also need the scalar product with the momentum transfer 𝐪\mathbf{q},

(𝐯el⟂⋅𝐪)|𝐤=𝟎\displaystyle(\mathbf{v}_{\rm el}^{\perp}\cdot\mathbf{q})|_{\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{0}} =Δ​E1→2+q22​mχ−q22​μe\displaystyle=\Delta E_{1\rightarrow 2}+\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{\chi}}-\frac{q^{2}}{2\mu_{e}}
=Δ​E1→2−q22​me.\displaystyle=\Delta E_{1\rightarrow 2}-\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{e}}\,. (129)

For the last two relations, we used energy conservation via Eq. (121). The dependence on the binding energies via Δ​E1→2\Delta E_{1\rightarrow 2} also explains why the DM response functions Rin​ℓR_{i}^{n\ell} carry the atomic quantum numbers (n​ℓ)(n\ell) as indices.

Appendix D Anapole, magnetic and electric dipole dark matter

The anapole, magnetic dipole and electric dipole DM models are described by the following interaction Lagrangians

ℒanapole\displaystyle\mathscr{L}_{\rm anapole} =g2​Λ2​χ¯​γμ​γ5​χ​∂νFμ​ν,\displaystyle=\frac{g}{2\Lambda^{2}}\,\overline{\chi}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{5}\chi\,\partial^{\nu}F_{\mu\nu}\,, (130)
ℒmagnetic\displaystyle\mathscr{L}_{\rm magnetic} =gΛ​ψ¯​σμ​ν​ψ​Fμ​ν,\displaystyle=\frac{g}{\Lambda}\,\overline{\psi}\sigma^{\mu\nu}\psi\,F_{\mu\nu}\,, (131)
ℒelectric\displaystyle\mathscr{L}_{\rm electric} =gΛ​i​ψ¯​σμ​ν​γ5​ψ​Fμ​ν,\displaystyle=\frac{g}{\Lambda}\,i\overline{\psi}\sigma^{\mu\nu}\gamma^{5}\psi\,F_{\mu\nu}\,, (132)

where χ\chi (ψ\psi) is a Majorana (Dirac) spinor describing the DM particle, gg a dimensionless coupling constant and Λ\Lambda a mass scale. For simplicity, we use the same notation for the coupling constants of the three interactions, but they can in principle be different. The Lagrangians in Eq. (132) induce a DM-electron coupling via the electromagnetic current, JνJ^{\nu}, and Maxwell equations, ∂μFμ​ν=e​Jν\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=eJ^{\nu}, where ψe\psi_{e} is the four component electron spinor, Fμ​ν=∂μAν−∂νAμF_{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu}-\partial_{\nu}A_{\mu} is the photon field strength tensor, and AνA^{\nu} the photon field.

Taking the nonrelativistic limit of the free field solution of the equations of motion for ψ\psi (or χ\chi), and using Gordon’s identity to express the matrix element of the current JνJ^{\nu} between single particle electron states in terms of electromagnetic form factors, at leading order we find the following amplitudes for DM scattering by free electrons

ℳanapole\displaystyle\mathscr{M}_{\rm anapole} =4​e​gΛ2mχme{2(𝐯el⟂⋅ξ†s′𝐒χξs)δλ′​λ\displaystyle=\frac{4eg}{\Lambda^{2}}m_{\chi}m_{e}\Bigg\{2\left(\mathbf{v}_{\rm el}^{\perp}\cdot\xi^{\dagger s^{\prime}}\mathbf{S}_{\chi}\xi^{s}\right)\delta^{\lambda^{\prime}\lambda}
+ge(ξ†s′𝐒χξs)⋅(i𝐪me×ξ†λ′𝐒eξλ)},\displaystyle+g_{e}\left(\xi^{\dagger s^{\prime}}\mathbf{S}_{\chi}\xi^{s}\right)\cdot\left(i\frac{\mathbf{q}}{m_{e}}\times\xi^{\dagger\lambda^{\prime}}\mathbf{S}_{e}\xi^{\lambda}\right)\Bigg\}\,, (133)
ℳmagnetic\displaystyle\mathscr{M}_{\rm magnetic} =e​gΛ{4meδs′​sδλ′​λ\displaystyle=\frac{eg}{\Lambda}\Bigg\{4m_{e}\delta^{s^{\prime}s}\delta^{\lambda^{\prime}\lambda}
+16​mχ​meq2i𝐪⋅(𝐯el⟂×ξ†s′𝐒χξs)δλ′​λ\displaystyle+\frac{16m_{\chi}m_{e}}{q^{2}}i\mathbf{q}\cdot\left(\mathbf{v}_{\rm el}^{\perp}\times\xi^{\dagger s^{\prime}}\mathbf{S}_{\chi}\xi^{s}\right)\delta^{\lambda^{\prime}\lambda}
−8​ge​mχq2[(𝐪⋅ξ†s′𝐒χξs)(𝐪⋅ξ†λ′𝐒eξλ)\displaystyle-\frac{8g_{e}m_{\chi}}{q^{2}}\Bigg[\left(\mathbf{q}\cdot\xi^{\dagger s^{\prime}}\mathbf{S}_{\chi}\xi^{s}\right)\left(\mathbf{q}\cdot\xi^{\dagger\lambda^{\prime}}\mathbf{S}_{e}\xi^{\lambda}\right)
−q2(ξ†s′𝐒χξs)⋅(ξ†λ′𝐒eξλ)]},\displaystyle-q^{2}\left(\xi^{\dagger s^{\prime}}\mathbf{S}_{\chi}\xi^{s}\right)\cdot\left(\xi^{\dagger\lambda^{\prime}}\mathbf{S}_{e}\xi^{\lambda}\right)\Bigg]\Bigg\}\,, (134)
ℳelectric\displaystyle\mathscr{M}_{\rm electric} =e​gΛ​16​mχ​meq2​i​𝐪⋅(ξ†s′​𝐒χ​ξs)​δλ′​λ.\displaystyle=\frac{eg}{\Lambda}\frac{16m_{\chi}m_{e}}{q^{2}}i\mathbf{q}\cdot\left(\xi^{\dagger s^{\prime}}\mathbf{S}_{\chi}\xi^{s}\right)\delta^{\lambda^{\prime}\lambda}\,. (135)

Here, the notation is the same one used in the main body of the paper. Matching these expressions on to the effective theory expansion in Eq. (19), one can express the effective coupling constants given in Sec. IV.2 in terms of gg and Λ\Lambda. In the numerical calculations, we set ge=2g_{e}=2.

Appendix E Details of direct detection and exclusion limits

The exclusion limits presented in this paper are based on a re-interpretation of published data and results by DarkSide-50 [12], XENON10 [43], and XENON1T [15]. In this section, we briefly summarize the necessary details to compute the exclusion limits.

An essential input for the prediction of ionization rates is the local density and velocity distribution of the DM particles of the galactic halo, which first enters Eq. (13). The local DM number density is simply given by

nχ=ρχmχ,\displaystyle n_{\chi}=\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\,, (136)

where we set ρχ=0.4​ GeV/cm3\rho_{\chi}=~0.4\text{ GeV/cm}^{3} [65]. For the velocity distribution, we use the standard halo model (SHM) which approximates the distribution by a truncated Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution that has been boosted into the Earth’s rest frame,

fχ​(𝐯)\displaystyle f_{\chi}(\mathbf{v}) =1Nesc​π3/2​v03​exp⁡[−(𝐯+𝐯⊕)2v02]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{\rm esc}\pi^{3/2}v_{0}^{3}}\exp\left[-\frac{(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{v}_{\oplus})^{2}}{v_{0}^{2}}\right]
×Θ⁡(vesc−|𝐯+𝐯⊕|).\displaystyle\times\Theta\left(v_{\rm esc}-|\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{v}_{\oplus}|\right)\,. (137)

Here, Nesc≡erf(vesc/v0)−2(vesc/v0)exp(−vesc2/v02)/πN_{\rm esc}\equiv\mathop{\mathrm{erf}}(v_{\rm esc}/v_{0})-2(v_{\rm esc}/v_{0})\exp(-v_{\rm esc}^{2}/v_{0}^{2})/\sqrt{\pi} is a normalization constant, and the standard choices for the other parameters are v0=220​km sec−1v_{0}=220\text{km sec}^{-1} for the Sun’s circular velocity [66], and vesc=544​km sec−1v_{\rm esc}=544\text{km sec}^{-1} for the galactic escape velocity [67]. For the speed of the Earth/the observer in the galactic rest frame, we choose v⊕≈244​km sec−1v_{\oplus}\approx 244\text{km sec}^{-1}.

In all cases, we have to translate the energy spectrum given in Eq. (30) into the spectrum as a function of the number of final electrons nen_{e},

d​ℛionn​ℓd​ne=∫d​Ee​P​(ne|Ee)​d​ℛionn​ℓd​Ee.\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathscr{R}_{\rm ion}^{n\ell}}{\mathrm{d}n_{e}}=\int\mathrm{d}E_{e}\;\mathrm{P}(n_{e}|E_{e})\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathscr{R}_{\rm ion}^{n\ell}}{\mathrm{d}E_{e}}\,. (138)

In modeling the probability P⁡(ne|Ee)\mathrm{P}(n_{e}|E_{e}) for nen_{e} electrons to reach the gas phase of the TPC given an initial electron energy of EeE_{e}, we follow [13, 14].

For the three experiments, we obtain the 90% C.L. exclusion limits by applying Poisson statistics to each event bin independently.

E.1 XENON10 and XENON1T

For XENON10 and XENON1T, the number of observed signals given in bins of the ionization signal (S2) are available and listed in Table 2. It is necessary to have the spectrum in terms of S2, i.e. the number of photoelectrons (PEs) in the photomultiplier tubes,

d​ℛionn​ℓdS2=ε⁡(S​2)​∑ne=1∞P⁡(S​2|ne)​d​ℛionn​ℓd​ne.\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathscr{R}_{\rm ion}^{n\ell}}{\mathrm{d}\mathrm{S2}}=\varepsilon(S2)\sum_{n_{e}=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{P}(S2|n_{e})\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathscr{R}_{\rm ion}^{n\ell}}{\mathrm{d}n_{e}}\,. (139)

For a given number of electrons nen_{e}, we assume that the resulting number of PEs follows a Gaussian distribution with mean ne​g2n_{e}g_{2} and width ne​σS​2\sqrt{n_{e}}\sigma_{S2} [68, 14, 69],

P⁡(S​2|ne)\displaystyle\mathrm{P}(S2|n_{e}) =Gauss⁡(S​2|ne​g2,ne​σS​2).\displaystyle=\mathrm{Gauss}(S2|n_{e}g_{2},\sqrt{n_{e}}\sigma_{S2})\,. (140)

The used parameters for the distribution’s mean and width are the secondary-scintillation gain factor g2=27​(33)g_{2}=27(33) and the associated width factor σS​2=6.7​(7)\sigma_{S2}=6.7(7) for XENON10 (XENON1T)[70, 14, 15, 71].

For XENON10, the binned observed numbers of events are given on the left hand side of Table 2, which correspond to an exposure of 15 kg days. The efficiency ε⁡(S​2)\varepsilon(S2) is given by the product of a flat cut efficiency of 92% [43] multiplied by the trigger efficiency given in Fig. 1 of [13].

In the case of XENON1T, we extracted the number of observed events passing all the cuts from Fig. 3 of [15]. They are listed on the right side of Table 2. The efficiency ε⁡(S​2)\varepsilon(S2) is the product of a flat efficiency of 93% and the different efficiencies given in Fig. 2 of [15]1313 13 Note that the ‘radius’ efficiency needs to be squared.. The exposure ℰ\mathcal{E} is given by

ℰ=R2​π×Δ​z×ρXe×Δ​t,\displaystyle\mathcal{E}=R^{2}\pi\times\Delta z\times\rho_{\rm Xe}\times\Delta t\,, (141)

where the target’s radius is R=47.9R=47.9cm, the height of the search’s volume is Δ​z=20\Delta z=20cm (corresponding to z∈[−30​cm,−10​cm]z\in[-30\mathrm{cm},-10\mathrm{cm}]), the density of liquid xenon is taken to be ρXe=3.1​g​cm−3\rho_{\rm Xe}=3.1\mathrm{g\;cm}^{-3}, and the time of the search data Δ​t=180.7\Delta t=180.7 days [15]. This yields an exposure of ∼\sim 80755 kg days.

Compared to the official XENON1T limits on the standard DM-electron scattering cross section (corresponding to our effective coupling c1c_{1}), our constraints are weaker by a factor of a few and therefore conservative, which can potentially be explained by the additional background subtraction the XENON collaboration performs.

E.2 DarkSide-50

Just like XENON10 and XENON1T, DarkSide is a dual-phase TPC. However, instead of xenon, it uses argon as target [20]. The DarkSide-50 experiment had an exposure of 6786 kg days, and a threshold of ne=3n_{e}=3 electrons. The number of observed events we base our limits on have been extracted from Fig. 3 of [20]. The official constraints on the standard DM-electron interaction (corresponding to the effective coupling c1c_{1}) turn out to be stronger than our own limits by a factor of a few.
